inline.s: The mani pearl that man does not know is gathered and kept within the Tathagata-garbha.
Six divine functions, empty yet not empty; a single orb of perfect light, colored yet not colored.

The wish-fulfilling jewel, which people do not know, is within the Tathagata-garbha. Once this mani pearl is found, the six faculties become liberated (the six divine functions). This six-fold divine function of the six faculties being liberated is empty and yet not empty; the orb of light of the mani pearl is colored and yet not colored.

Mani pearl (mo ni zhu): the wish-fulfilling jewel; here it is a metaphor for the wondrous function that appears after one realizes the Tathagata-garbha. Tathagata-garbha (ru lai zang): the original nature. As for the Tathagata-garbha,
see in detail
Mind, Self-nature, and Tathagata-garbha
Six divine functions (liu ban shen yong): the wondrous function in which the six faculties (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind) become liberated. The Surangama Sutra says:
“When one faculty returns to its source, the six faculties become liberated.”

Six divine functions, empty and not empty (liu ban shen yong kong, bu kong): the six divine functions, viewed from principle, are empty; viewed from phenomena, they are not empty. One orb of perfect light, colored yet not colored (yi ke yuan guang se fei se): the orb of light of the mani pearl, viewed from principle, is not colored; viewed from phenomena, it is colored.
Purify the five eyes and attain the five powers; only through personal realization can one know, hard to fathom!
To see forms in a mirror is not hard; to seize the moon in water, how could one grasp it?

The state of purifying the five eyes and attaining the five powers can only be known through one’s own personal realization (not through speculation). People regard the cultivation of a realized one as if looking at forms in a mirror: to imitate him on the surface is not difficult, but it is like grasping the moon in water — one cannot obtain the moon. Only by doing the practice from the very root oneself, and personally realizing it, is one on the right path.

Purify the five eyes (jing wu yan): the flesh eye is not deluded by objects; the divine eye sees through to all things; the wisdom eye’s insight is clear and penetrating; the Dharma eye sees that nature is originally empty; the Buddha eye regards things and self with equality. Attain the five powers (de wu li): once the five eyes are purified, the five powers naturally manifest before one. The five powers (wu li): the power of faith, the power of vigor, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom. The power of faith can destroy all evil beliefs; the power of vigor can destroy the laziness of the body; the power of mindfulness can destroy all evil thoughts; the power of concentration can destroy all confused imaginings; and the power of wisdom can destroy all the delusions of the three realms. Only through personal realization can one know, hard to fathom (wei zheng nai zhi nan ke ce): the gate of the ground of mind can only be known through realization, and cannot be measured by the feelings of ordinary beings. To see forms in a mirror is not hard, to seize the moon in water how could one grasp it (jing li kan xing jian bu nan, shui zhong zhuo yue zen nian de): it is said that whenever Einstein gave a lecture, his chauffeur sat in the back row, listening intently and taking notes. One day the chauffeur said to Einstein: “I too could give your lecture.” Einstein said: “Very well, next time you deliver it for me.” So, with Einstein’s consent, the chauffeur joyfully gave a fluent lecture. Just as he was triumphantly concluding, the audience began to ask questions, and the chauffeur was dumbfounded. There is a similar matter in the Chan school: when Master Dahui went to Fujian to guide Chan practitioners, he found that each and every one of them spoke remarkably, and he was greatly astonished. Upon questioning, they admitted: “We have memorized these from the Blue Cliff Record; we have not, in fact, awakened.” (This is treating the old masters’ cases as ready-made replies, taking clever advantage, and applying them solely to deal with the examinations of a student’s studied practice.) Panshan says:
“The one road on high, the thousand sages do not transmit; the student wears out his body, as a monkey grasping for its shadow.”
(From the Transmission of the Lamp)
Constantly walking alone, constantly solitary in step, the attained ones roam together the road of nirvana.
His tune is ancient, his spirit pure, his manner of itself is lofty; his face gaunt, his bones firm, yet men do not regard him.

He constantly walks alone, constantly solitary in step, roaming together with the awakened upon the road that leads to nirvana. His bearing is lofty and antique, his mind clear and serene, and his manner in the Way is naturally noble. Yet his countenance is worn and his bones are firm, and worldly people pay him no heed.
Roam (you): to walk calmly and at ease.
The poor son of the Buddha, in word calls himself poor; in truth his body is poor, his Way is not poor.
Being poor, his body is ever clad in tattered wool; possessing the Way, his heart conceals the priceless jewel.

The poor son of the Buddha, in word calls himself a poor monk; in truth his body is poor and his Way is rich. His body being poor, he is ever clad in ragged clothes; his Way being rich, his heart stores the priceless jewel.
Son of the Buddha (shi zi): a disciple of Sakyamuni Buddha; this is the general term for members of the sangha. Lu he (
lu he
): torn, ragged clothes.
The priceless jewel, its use is never exhausted; benefiting things and responding to occasions, it never hoards.
In the body, the three bodies and the four wisdoms are perfectly complete; in the ground of mind, the eight liberations and the six superknowledges are stamped.

The priceless jewel, its use without end; it benefits all things and, responding to occasions, is given without the least stinginess. In the body the three bodies and the four wisdoms are complete; in the ground of mind the eight liberations and the six superknowledges are stamped.

The eight liberations (ba jie): namely the eight samadhi-releases: first, having thoughts of form, one contemplates the objects of form — this is the liberation. Second, with no thought of form inwardly, one contemplates outer forms — this is the liberation. Third, the pure liberation where one attains bodily witness and dwells in its completeness — this is the liberation. Fourth, the liberation of the sphere of infinite space. Fifth, the liberation of the sphere of infinite consciousness. Sixth, the liberation of the sphere of nothing whatsoever. Seventh, the liberation of the sphere of neither perception nor non-perception. Eighth, the liberation of the cessation of perception and feeling, where one attains bodily witness and dwells in its completeness. The three bodies (san shen): the Dharma-body, the reward-body, and the response-body. The Dharma-body, also called the self-nature body, or the Dharma-nature body, is originally possessed by everyone; only we sentient beings are deluded and do not reveal it, whereas the Buddha is awakened and has realized it. The reward-body is formed of the Buddha’s wisdom and merit, and is distinguished as the reward-body of self-enjoyment and the reward-body of other-enjoyment: the reward-body of self-enjoyment is the body in which the Buddha himself enjoys the joy of the Dharma realized within; the reward-body of other-enjoyment is the body manifested by the Buddha to speak the Dharma to the bodhisattvas of the ten grounds. The response-body, also called the accommodating transformation body, or the metamorphic body, is the Buddha-body manifested in response to the opportunities and conditions of sentient beings. The four wisdoms (si zhi): the wisdom of accomplished action, the wisdom of wondrous contemplation, the wisdom of equality, and the great mirror wisdom. The wisdom of accomplished action is accomplished by transforming the five fallen-and-defiled consciousnesses (the eye-, ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-consciousnesses), and is the Buddha’s wisdom that accomplishes all deeds benefiting all sentient beings. The wisdom of wondrous contemplation is accomplished by transforming the sixth fallen-and-defiled consciousness (the mind-consciousness), and is the Buddha’s wisdom that observes all dharmas and the capacities of all sentient beings, and gives the medicine according to the illness and transforms the ordinary into the sage. The wisdom of equality is accomplished by transforming the seventh fallen-and-defiled consciousness (the manas), and is the Buddha’s wisdom that penetrates the principle of selflessness and equality, and on that account raises the great compassion without conditions toward all sentient beings. The great mirror wisdom is accomplished by transforming the eighth fallen-and-defiled consciousness (the alaya), and is the Buddha’s wisdom that contemplates all phenomena and principles without anything not understood; this wisdom, pure and clear, sees through to both inner and outer, like a great round mirror, illuminating all things.
The superior man, once resolved, is done with all; the middling and the lower, though much learned, do not believe.
But when one alone unbinds the soiled garment from within his own breast, who can boast of vigor toward the outside?

The superior man realizes the true reality of all dharmas (once resolved), and being once resolved, is done with all; but many of the middling and lower sort, on hearing it, do not believe. One can only personally cut off ignorance and realize the original nature — how then can it be proclaimed outwards to others?
Once resolved (yi jue): this is the “realizing the true reality” spoken of earlier. Done with all (yi qie le): the earlier song says:
“Realize the true reality, and there is neither person nor dharma.”

Because one has realized the true reality of all dharmas, both the attachment to person and the attachment to dharma are cut off, and of course all is done. Therefore this is an extremely perfect and sudden gate, cutting straight to the very root. Unbinding the soiled garment (jie gou yi): cutting off ignorance and realizing the original nature (the Tathagata-garbha). The Lankavatara Sutra says:
“The Tathagata-garbha is pure in its own nature, and turns the thirty-two marks to enter into the bodies of all sentient beings. Like a great precious gem wrapped in a soiled garment.”
Let him slander, let him condemn; to set fire to the sky only wearies oneself in vain.

When I hear it, it is like drinking sweet dew; melting away, I suddenly enter the inconceivable. Even if the iron wheel whirled above my head, the perfect light of concentration and wisdom is never lost.

People not only do not believe in this perfect and sudden gate, but on the contrary revile and slander it. If one pays them no heed (let him slander, let him condemn), these revilings and slanders are like raising fire to burn the sky — they burn nothing, and dying away of themselves, merely waste effort. When I hear these revilings and slanders, it is like drinking the sweet dew; after melting away the self-nature, I suddenly enter the inconceivable state. Even if the iron wheel whirled above my head, the perfect light of concentration and wisdom is never for a moment lost.

Let him slander, let him condemn (cong ta bang, ren ta fei): allow him to revile, allow him to oppose. Master Shenhui, the author of the Song of the Realization of the Way, in order to spread the Sixth Patriarch’s sudden teaching, endured slander, defamation, and persecution.
According to the record:

Shenhui, fond of study from a young age, heard that the great master of Caoxi in Lingnan was greatly exalting the Way of Chan, and so, emulating Sudhana’s fifty-three pilgrimages, he traveled from afar, not shunning a thousand li, to pay homage to the Sixth Patriarch; his feet were torn and he had no shoes, so he tore his clothes to wrap his feet and went on. After seeing the patriarch, he attended upon him constantly and received the sudden teaching in full. The Sixth Patriarch praised him, saying:
“Little Master Shenhui, you have attained that good and not-good are equal, that praise and blame move you not, that sorrow and joy are not born.”
(From the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch
the tenth chapter, the Chapter of Entrustment)

Although Huineng, having received the robe and bowl of the Fifth Patriarch Hongren, became the Sixth Patriarch, his sudden teaching spread only within the Lingnan region alone. In all the vast land of China, it was almost entirely the world of Shenxiu’s gradual teaching. After Shenxiu passed away, his great disciple Puji continued to propagate his lineage, flourishing for a time, and the people of the day called him “the master of the Dharma in the two capitals, the teacher of the three emperors” (the two capitals referring to the western capital Chang’an and the eastern capital Luoyang, and the three emperors to Empress Wu Zetian, Emperor Zhongzong, and Emperor Ruizong). Puji also regarded Shenxiu as the orthodox heir of Bodhidharma’s school, and established him as the Sixth Patriarch, while calling himself the Seventh Patriarch.

In order to protect the right Dharma, Shenhui entered the capital city of Luoyang, and, heedless of the threat to his very life, made the lion’s roar, greatly propagating the Chan Dharma of Caoxi. He established an open, unhindered assembly at the Dayun Monastery in Huatai, Henan, and openly engaged in debate with Master Chongyuan, then renowned in both capitals and known even beyond the sea, concerning the right and wrong, the true and the false, of the southern and northern schools of Chan. He attacked the northern school for “borrowed transmission and gradual practice,” and wrote the Record of Illuminating the Essential Doctrine, determining the southern Huineng as the sudden school (definitively establishing the southern Huineng as the sudden school) and the northern Shenxiu as the gradual teaching (the northern Shenxiu as the gradual teaching). Establishing the essential purport of the southern school, he caused the sudden teaching to be greatly spread in Luoyang and to circulate throughout the empire, a bright lamp shining high, generation after generation transformed by it.

Heedless of the threat to his very life, making the lion’s roar (bu gu xing ming wei xie zuo shi zi hou): according to the record in the Treatise Determining Right and Wrong in the Southern School, at the time Chongyuan threatened Shenhui, saying: “Master Puji’s name covers the whole land, known throughout the world, proclaimed by every mouth, and beyond thought. To criticize him in this way, is this not to make an enemy of your own body and life?” Shenhui answered: “Master Puji’s school differs from the southern school; I myself weigh the right and wrong and determine its essential purport. I now say that to spread the Mahayana and establish the right Dharma, causing all sentient beings to know and hear it — how could I begrudge my body and life?” Chongyuan again asked: “In doing this, is it not to seek fame and profit?” Shenhui answered: “I do not spare even my life; how could I be concerned with fame and profit?” This fully shows Shenhui’s spirit of forgetting his body for the sake of the Dharma. For this reason, Shenhui suffered the jealousy and wrongs of the northern school to the utmost; the censor Lü Yi, currying favor with Puji, falsely accused Shenhui of gathering disciples, suspecting him of fomenting trouble. According to the Great Commentary on the Surangama Sutra, Shenhui, within less than two years, was forced to move his dwelling four times: “In the twelfth year of the Tianbao era, being slandered as gathering a crowd, an edict banished him to Yiyang Commandery, and then moved him to Wudang Commandery. By the thirteenth year, by imperial grace, he was moved to Xiangzhou. By the seventh month, another edict moved him to Kaiyuan Monastery in Jingzhou. All of this was the destruction carried out by members of the northern school.” In the third year of Shenhui’s banishment, the situation suddenly changed, and the rebellion of An and Shi broke out; Lü Yi was killed by the rebels, and only then did the persecution cease. The unhindered assembly (wu zhe hui): this kind of assembly makes offerings indiscriminately to all, as people today hold a thousand-monk feast to form bonds with ten thousand persons; anyone may take part, without any bar or restriction.
Regarding evil words as merit, this becomes to me a good teacher.
If enmity and kinship did not arise through mockery and slander, how could one show the compassionate endurance-power of the unborn?

To regard (to view) evil words as merit: this is the good teacher who perfects me. If it were not that enmity and kinship arise on account of reviling and slander, how could I manifest the compassionate endurance-power of the unborn (the realization that all dharmas are wholly empty and still), in which enmity and kinship are equal?
Mockery and slander (shan
shan
bang): mocking (to ridicule and sneer) and defamation.

blocks.text: Five: Through in Both the Essential and the Expounded

inline.s: Through in the essential and through in the expounded, the perfect light of concentration and wisdom does not dwell in emptiness.
Not only have I now alone thoroughly arrived; the bodies of all the Buddhas numerous as the sands of the Ganges are also the same.

I am through in both the essential and the expounded, with the perfect light of concentration and wisdom, not dwelling in emptiness. Not only have I now alone thoroughly arrived; the Buddhas numerous as the sands of the Ganges have also realized the essence in this way.

Through in both the essential and the expounded (zong shuo ju tong): one who penetrates the profound essential purport in the Chan school is called through in the essential; one who can face the assembly and freely preach the teaching to transform beings is called through in the expounded. One who is through in both the essential and the expounded is a great master. The Lankavatara Sutra says:
“The Buddha told Mahamati: All sravakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas have two aspects of penetration, called the essential penetration and the expounded penetration.”
The commentary says: “The essential is the root of the Way; the expounded is the trace of the teaching.”
The lion’s roar, the fearless teaching; the hundred beasts, hearing it, all split with terror.
The fragrant elephant in flight loses his majesty; the dragons and devas listen in stillness and are filled with joy.

The lion’s roar, the fearless teaching; the hundred beasts are terrified out of their wits (their gall is burst). The fragrant elephant, in flight, loses his majesty; the dragons and devas, listening in stillness, are filled with joy.

The lion’s roar, the fearless teaching (shi zi hou, wu wei shuo): see the annotation “heedless of the threat to his very life, making the lion’s roar” above. The hundred beasts (bai shou): these refer to the disciples and followers of Master Puji. These men held great power in the western capital Chang’an and the eastern capital Luoyang, reaching from the imperial court on high down to the government offices, gentry, and officials below. The fragrant elephant (xiang xiang): the mighty and robust elephant, from the bones at its ear-gate secretes a liquid of fragrant scent, being much mightier and more robust than the ordinary elephant. Here it refers to Master Puji, “the master of the Dharma in the two capitals, the teacher of the three emperors.” The dragons and devas (tian long): the devas and dragons; here they refer to the bodhisattvas who have greatly opened up the perfect understanding.
Wandering the rivers and seas, crossing the mountains and streams, seeking a teacher and visiting the Way for the sake of Chan.
Ever since I recognized the road of Caoxi, I know that birth and death are no longer my concern.

Wandering the rivers and seas, crossing the mountains and streams, seeking a teacher and visiting the Way for the sake of Chan. Ever since I recognized the road of Caoxi (the Sixth Patriarch’s sudden teaching), I know that birth and death are no longer my concern (only then did I know that birth and death are but an illusion).
Walking is Chan, sitting is Chan; in speaking, in silence, in motion and stillness, the body is at ease.
Even meeting the sharp blade, one is ever serene; even were poison brought, it, too, is a thing of no account.
My teacher, having met Dipamkara Buddha, for many aeons was the ascetic of patient endurance.]

Walking too is in Chan, sitting too is in Chan; whether speaking (words) or silent (no words), whether moving or still, all is serene and at ease. Even if the sharp blade is laid upon me, I am likewise calm; even if poison schemes against me, it is a thing of no account. The reason my teacher (Sakyamuni Buddha) met Dipamkara Buddha is that for many aeons he had been the ascetic of patient endurance.

This is the true portrayal of Master Shenhui’s mind and conduct amid exile and persecution. In former days, Master Hanshan, having met with trouble on account of spreading the Dharma, was cast into the imperial dungeon; when life and death were yet undecided, he did not diminish even one thought of joy — this too is the same state. Master Hanshan wrote: “In recent days, because I spread the Dharma I fell into persecution, and the emperor was greatly enraged (the master, being slandered for spreading the Dharma, enraged the sovereign, was arrested and cast into prison, tortured with severe punishment, with life and death undecided), like a bolt from a clear sky, at which hearers stopped their ears. From my arrest until the exile from the capital, for more than two hundred days I experienced every hardship, beyond all words. From first to last, I beheld the one thought of joy within me, and it was not in the least diminished from usual; those who saw it were all greatly astonished. As for the sudden calamity of life and death, by it others were alarmed on my account; but when they saw my joy undiminished from its usual state, they were the more astonished. I am not astonished at the calamity of life and death at which men are astonished, while men are astonished that I am not astonished — perhaps there is some principle in it!” (The original is found in the Collected Works from the Dream Wanderings
in “Shown to the Attendant Qi on the Boat to Leiyang”)

Serene (tan tan): perfectly calm. Even were (jia rao): even if, granting that. Of no account (xian xian): trifling, as a casual thing. The ascetic of patient endurance (ren ru xian): Sakyamuni Buddha, in his causal stage, was the ascetic of patient endurance, cultivating the practice of patience. In the Diamond Sutra, the Buddha says:

“Subhuti! Further, reflect on the past, when for five hundred lives I was the ascetic of patient endurance. In those lives I had no mark of self, no mark of person, no mark of sentient beings, and no mark of a life.”
This chapter says:
“My teacher
(Sakyamuni Buddha)
, having met Dipamkara Buddha, for many aeons was the ascetic of patient endurance.”
From this it can be seen that the practice of patient endurance is the foremost wondrous practice for attaining Buddhahood.
How many times born, how many times dead; drifting through birth and death, with no certain rest.
Ever since suddenly awakening to the unborn, what sorrow or joy is there in honor and disgrace?

Master Shenhui had passed through birth and death many times; whether to live or to die, his future was undecided (hard to foresee). But ever since he suddenly awakened to the unborn Dharma, what is there to sorrow or to rejoice in honor, disgrace, birth, and death?
Entering the deep mountains, dwelling in the aranya, beneath the steep, secluded, and ancient pines
at ease in silent sitting in the wild monk’s home; dwelling in profound quiet, truly free and easy.
Entering the deep mountains and dwelling in the aranya, beneath the steep and distant old pines, is the home of the wild monk who sits at ease; to dwell here in quiet peace is truly free and easy.
This paragraph describes the situation of dwelling in the mountains after one has attained the purport.
Aranya (lan ruo): the abbreviation of aranya, a place where monks practice in quietness. Cen yin (
cen yin
): the steep, lofty appearance of the mountains. You sui (
sui
): a remote, distant place. Qu (
qu
ji): quiet and still.

blocks.text: Six: When One Awakens, It Is Done

inline.s: When one awakens, it is done, with no exertion applied; it is unlike all conditioned dharmas.
Clinging
to marks, giving brings the blessing of heavenly rebirth, like shooting an arrow upward at the empty sky.

When one awakens, it is done, with no exertion applied (this is the unconditioned Dharma), and is unlike all conditioned dharmas. Giving while clinging to marks (a conditioned Dharma) at most attains the blessing of heavenly rebirth; this is like raising one’s head and shooting an arrow at the empty sky.

When one awakens, it is done, with no exertion applied (jue ji le, bu shi gong): having awakened to the true reality of all dharmas, then all is done, and there is no further need to apply effort to any practice; it is the effortless practice. Effortless practice (wu gong yong xing): to practice without borrowing the three of body, speech, and mind, moving freely and spontaneously in a natural state. Conditioned dharmas (you wei fa): ordinarily, conditioned dharmas refer to all things produced by the union of conditions. Here conditioned dharmas are spoken of in regard to cultivation. Cultivation is divided into conditioned dharmas and unconditioned dharmas: to practice while clinging to marks is a conditioned Dharma; to practice while free from marks is an unconditioned Dharma. For example, if the mind abides in dharmas (clinging to marks) and practices giving, this is a conditioned Dharma; if the mind does not abide in dharmas (free from marks) and practices giving, this is an unconditioned Dharma. The Diamond Sutra says:
“If a bodhisattva’s mind abides in dharmas
(clinging to marks)
and he practices giving, it is like a man entering darkness
(the same as “darkness”)
, and he sees nothing. If a bodhisattva’s mind does not abide in dharmas
(free from marks)
and he practices giving, it is like a man with eyes, whose sight the light of the sun illumines, and he sees all manner of forms.”
It also says:
“All the sages and holy ones differ only by virtue of the unconditioned Dharma.”
(See in detail
The Diamond Sutra Explained
In the Sutra of Forty-Two Sections spoken by the Buddha, it is said:

“The Buddha said: A renunciant who has left home cuts off desire and abandons love, recognizes the source of his own mind, reaches the Buddha’s profound principle, and understands the unconditioned Dharma. Inwardly he has nothing attained; outwardly he seeks nothing; his mind is not bound to the Way
(not clinging to the Way)
, nor does it create karma
(nor does it generate karma)
; with no thought and no doing, neither practicing nor realizing
(practicing without practice, realizing without realization)
Without passing through the stages
(without passing through the fifty-two stages)
, yet of himself he is supremely honored; this is called the Way.”
(See in detail
Annotation to the Sutra of Forty-Two Sections

The fifty-two stages (wu shi er ge jie wei): a bodhisattva’s practice has fifty-two stages: the ten faiths, the ten abodes, the ten practices, the ten dedications, the ten grounds, the stage of equal enlightenment, and the stage of wondrous enlightenment; the stage of wondrous enlightenment is Buddhahood.

Clinging to marks (zhuo xiang): to take marks as real, and so to love and hate, to take and reject. Giving while clinging to marks (zhuo xiang bu shi): if, in giving, one realizes the three wheels as empty, this is mark-free giving, also called formless giving; if one does not, it is giving while clinging to marks, also called marked giving. The three wheels as empty (san lun ti kong): the giver, the receiver, and the thing given are called the three wheels. After giving, these three wheels’ marks are not retained in the mind; this is called “the three wheels as empty.”
Mark-free giving is endowed with the six perfections (the six paramitas). In the Mahaprajnaparamita Sutra
chapter one, the Introductory Chapter, the Buddha says:
“Sariputra! When a bodhisattva-mahasattva practices the perfection of giving in the prajna paramita
(that is, mark-free giving)
, by virtue of the power of his skillful wisdom he can be complete with the perfection of dana
(giving)
, the perfection of sila
(precept-keeping)
, the perfection of ksanti
(patience)
, the perfection of virya
(vigor)
, the perfection of dhyana
(meditation)
, and the perfection of prajna
(wisdom)

. Sariputra said to the Buddha: World-honored One, how is it that when a bodhisattva-mahasattva practices giving, by virtue of the power of his skillful wisdom he is complete with the perfection of dana and so on to the perfection of prajna? The Buddha told Sariputra: Because the giver, the receiver, and the goods are unobtainable
(the three wheels as empty)
, he is complete with the perfection of dana. Because the sinful and the sinless are unobtainable, he is complete with the perfection of sila. Because the mind is unmoved, he is complete with the
chan

perfection of ksanti. Because body and mind are vigorous and never slack, he is complete with the perfection of virya. Because he is neither scattered nor dull, he is complete with the perfection of dhyana. Because he knows all dharmas as unobtainable, he is complete with the perfection of prajna.”
In the Great Prajna Paramita Sutra
chapter two, the Chapter on Studying and Contemplating, the Buddha says:

“The bodhisattvas-mahasattvas who cultivate the prajna paramita can thus for real know: if a bodhisattva-mahasattva, taking non-acquisition as his skillful means, cultivates the perfection of giving, and penetratively understands that all givers, all receivers, and all things given are unobtainable
(the three wheels as empty)
, then this giving, as a skillful and adroit means, can fulfill the perfections of giving, pure precepts, patience, vigor, meditation, and prajna.”

The six perfections (liu du): also called the six paramitas, the six practices by which one can cross from this shore of the suffering of birth and death to the other shore of the bliss of nirvana; namely, giving, precept-keeping, patience, vigor, meditation, and prajna. Giving ferries over stinginess and greed; precept-keeping ferries over transgression; patience ferries over anger; vigor ferries over sloth; meditation ferries over distraction; and prajna ferries over ignorance.

Giving while clinging to marks brings the blessing of heavenly rebirth (zhuo xiang bu shi sheng tian fu): giving while clinging to marks at most attains the blessing of heavenly rebirth and cannot escape the wheel of the six realms. The Pointing at the Moon Record says:
“Emperor Wu of Liang asked Bodhidharma
(Master Bodhidharma)
: ‘I have built monasteries and ordained monks without number — what merit is there in this?’
(What sort of merit is there? — Emperor Wu thought his merit was exceedingly great; he was clinging to marks.)
Bodhidharma said: ‘No merit.’ The emperor said: ‘Why is there no merit?’ Bodhidharma said: ‘This is but the small fruit of humans and devas
(this is merely the small retribution of being reborn as a human or a deva)
, a cause that is defiled. Like a shadow following the form, though it has being yet it is not real.”

Defiled (you lou): lou is another name for afflictions; the matter that contains afflictions (greed, anger, and ignorance) is called defiled; the matter free of afflictions is called undefiled. Merit (gong de): cultivation is the merit (gong); the purity of body and mind is the virtue (de); extinguishing the ignorance within the mind is the merit (gong); the manifestation of wisdom is the virtue (de). Blessedness (fu de): the portion of blessing gained by cultivating the wholesome acts of humans and devas. Blessedness and merit differ: the externally cultivated defiled good of worldly deeds is “blessedness,” while the inwardly realized undefiled wisdom of the Buddha-nature is “merit.” Moreover, in the cultivation of the Way, if one practices while clinging to marks, that is “blessedness”; if one practices while free from marks, that alone is “merit.”
When the force is spent, the arrow falls back down, summoning an unhappy next life.
How does it compare to the gate of the unconditioned true reality, which in one leap enters directly the ground of the Tathagata?

Once the arrow’s force is spent, it falls back down (this is a metaphor for the fact that once the blessings of heaven are exhausted one falls into the other five realms), summoning an unhappy next life. How does it compare to the gate of the unconditioned true reality, which, without passing through the stages, directly realizes Buddhahood?

How does it compare (zheng si): how can it be like. Summoning an unhappy next life (zhao de lai sheng bu ru yi): for if once the blessed retribution is exhausted, the next life is miserable. Hanshan says:

“I have seen the wheel-turning king, a thousand sons ever around him; by the ten wholesome deeds he transforms the four heavens, adorned with many precious things. The seven treasures ever accompany his person, adorned most wondrously and well. But once the blessed retribution is spent, it is like a
qi
bird among the reeds
(like a bird lodging in the reed thicket)
.— He will even become a worm upon the ox’s neck
(he will become an insect on the ox’s neck)
, receiving the karma-paths of the six destinies.”

(From the Collected Poems of the Master of Cold Mountain.) In one leap entering directly the ground of the Tathagata (yi chao zhi ru ru lai di): without passing through the stages, directly realizing Buddhahood. In the Sutra of Forty-Two Sections spoken by the Buddha, it is said:

“The Buddha said: A renunciant who has left home cuts off desire and abandons love, recognizes the source of his own mind, reaches the Buddha’s profound principle, and understands the unconditioned Dharma. Inwardly he has nothing attained; outwardly he seeks nothing; his mind is not bound to the Way
(not clinging to the Way)
, nor does it create karma
(nor does it generate karma)
; with no thought and no doing, neither practicing nor realizing
(practicing without practice, realizing without realization)
Without passing through the stages
(without passing through the fifty-two stages)
, yet of himself he is supremely honored; this is called the Way.”
Once you attain the root, do not worry over the branches; it is like pure lapis lazuli holding the precious moon.
Able to understand this wish-fulfilling jewel, benefiting self and others, it is never exhausted.

Once you attain the root (just realize the patient endurance of the unborn Dharma), do not worry over the branches (there is no need to be anxious about the miraculous functions and other branch-and-twig matters); then it is like pure lapis lazuli containing the precious moon (the perfectly bright, exquisite mind). Able to realize this perfectly bright, exquisite mind, the wish-fulfilling jewel, benefiting self and others will never be exhausted.
Like pure lapis lazuli holding the precious moon (ru jing liu li han bao yue): the Surangama Sutra says:

“If the aggregate of consciousness is exhausted, then the faculties present before you interfunction with one another. From this interfunctioning, one is able to enter the bodhisattva’s vajra-like, non-attached wisdom. The perfectly bright, exquisite mind then transforms and reveals within it, like pure lapis lazuli containing within it the precious moon. In this way one surmounts the ten faiths, the ten abodes, the ten practices, the ten dedications, the four stages of expedient aid, the ten vajra grounds practiced by the bodhisattva, and the perfect radiance of equal enlightenment, and enters the marvellous and adorned sea of the Tathagata.”

The river moon shines, the pine wind blows; through the long night and the clear evening, what is there to do? The Buddha-nature and the jewel of precepts are stamped in the ground of mind; mist, dew, clouds, and rosy clouds are the garments upon the body.

The bright moon over the river shines upon it, the wind through the pine wood blows; in this long night and clear evening, what is there to do? — The Buddha-nature and the jewel of precepts are stamped in the ground of mind; mist, dew, clouds, and rosy clouds are like the garments upon the body.
